Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Missed incidents, persistent threats, and response gaps: Insights from compromis
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,

| order by Timestamp desc

      AND (Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Windows\Fonts\Mysql*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Windows\System32\wbem*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/dev/null*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/var/folders/*" OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("nei.bat","dl1host.exe","bat.bat","cmd.bat","taskhost.exe","poab.bat","load.bat","loab.bat","mance.exe","eter.exe","puls.exe","eternalblue2.dll","doublepulsar2.dll","http.sys","scrcons.exe"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
| append [

      by Registry.dest, Registry.process_name, Registry.registry_path,

]

A dual United States and Estonian citizen has been extradited to the U.S. to face charges alleging he was a member of the Scattered Spider hacking collective. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Help-desk-driven password reset immediately followed by MFA re-registration (Scattered Spider account takeover) · [LLM] Genymotion/Genymobile Android emulator executing on a managed endpoint (Scattered Spider MFA tooling) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue federated domain / trust added to Entra tenant (Scattered Spider persistence) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → MFA fatigue / push-bombing · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Help-desk-driven password reset immediately followed by MFA re-registration (Scattered Spider account takeover) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the Scattered Spider initial-access pattern described in the luxury-retailer breach: attackers call IT help desk posing as employees to reset credentials, then register attacker-controlled MFA on the account. Correlates an Entra password-reset audit event with a security-info (MFA) registration for the same target within a short window. Rationale: Directly models the article's described luxury-retailer breach (helpdesk calls to reset credentials + gain admin access) plus the group's known MFA-registration hijack; the reset→MFA-register temporal correlation is far higher fidelity than either event alone. Cross-checked against CrowdStrike, ReliaQuest and CISA AA23-320a writeups of the same TTP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/defending-against-scattered-spider-with-falcon-next-gen-siem/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/scattered-spider-cyber-attacks-using-phishing-social-engineering-2025/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556.006 T1098.005
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate helpdesk password reset where the user then re-enrolls a lost/replaced phone for MFA
  • Onboarding of a new employee: admin resets temp password then user registers first MFA method
  • Bulk credential-hygiene campaign where IT forces resets and users re-register security info
  • Self-service password reset (SSPR) followed by the user updating their authenticator
  • Break-glass/admin account maintenance that legitimately re-provisions MFA
Suppression filter
| where MinutesApart <= 30 and ResetActor != TargetUpn   // attacker-driven resets are near-instant and actor != self
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the target UPN's sign-in history around ResetTime/MfaTime — check the IP/geo/device of the MFA registration vs the user's normal locations, and confirm with the user whether they requested the reset. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, revoke the user's refresh tokens, remove the newly registered MFA method, force a fresh reset with in-person/verified identity proofing, and disable the account if privileged. 3) Hunt: enumerate all actions by the account since MfaTime (role assignments, app consents, mailbox rules) and check for a follow-on 'Set domain authentication'/federation change (UC2) indicating persistence.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Change user password","User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration")
| summarize Ops = make_set(ActionType), Events = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Actors = make_set(AccountDisplayName), IPs = make_set(IPAddress) by ObjectName
| where Ops has_any ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Change user password") and Ops has_any ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration")
| order by LastSeen desc
let window = 1h;
let pwResets = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Change user password")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, ResetOp = OperationName, TargetUpn,
          ResetActor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
          ResetActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
let mfaReg = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration","User registered all required security info")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| project MfaTime = TimeGenerated, MfaOp = OperationName, TargetUpn,
          MfaActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
pwResets
| join kind=inner mfaReg on TargetUpn
| where MfaTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + window)   // MFA (re)registered within 1h of a reset = help-desk takeover shape
| project ResetTime, MfaTime,
          MinutesApart = datetime_diff('minute', MfaTime, ResetTime),
          TargetUpn, ResetOp, MfaOp, ResetActor, ResetActorIp, MfaActorIp
| order by ResetTime desc

Rogue federated domain / trust added to Entra tenant (Scattered Spider persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects an attacker converting or adding a domain to federated authentication (or adding an unverified domain) in Entra ID — the Octo Tempest/Scattered Spider backdoor that survives password resets by trusting an attacker-controlled IdP. Single-event, very low FP. Rationale: Federated-trust modification is the signature Scattered Spider/Octo Tempest cloud persistence mechanism confirmed across CrowdStrike and Microsoft; these Entra audit operation names are exact and near-zero legitimate frequency, making this an alert-grade single-event detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/defending-against-scattered-spider-with-falcon-next-gen-siem/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1484.002 T1556.007
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned M&A / tenant consolidation where IT legitimately federates a newly acquired domain to ADFS or a third-party IdP
  • Migration from managed to federated authentication (e.g. onboarding Okta/Ping as IdP)
  • Domain verification of a genuinely new company domain by a Global Admin
  • Scheduled ADFS-to-cloud or cloud-to-ADFS cutover maintenance
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the Actor and ActorIp performing the change — confirm it is a known Global/Hybrid Identity admin from an expected location, and verify a change ticket exists for the TargetDomain federation change. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, immediately revert the domain to managed authentication, remove the rogue federation/IdP trust, revoke the actor's sessions, and reset the actor's credentials + MFA. 3) Hunt: review all sign-ins asserting the affected domain's federation since the change, look for the reset→MFA-register precursor (UC1), and audit recent role assignments and OAuth app consents by the same actor.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("Set domain authentication","Set federation settings on domain","Add unverified domain")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ObjectName, ISP
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Set domain authentication","Set federation settings on domain","Add unverified domain")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
         ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress),
         TargetDomain = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIp, TargetDomain, Result, CorrelationId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Genymotion/Genymobile Android emulator executing on a managed endpoint (Scattered Spider MFA tooling) AIExploitation Low
Hunts for the Genymobile/Genymotion Android emulator the article attributes to Scattered Spider MFA attacks (used to stand up attacker-controlled virtual devices for push/authenticator registration). Flags emulator binaries or the vendor install path on corporate workstations where an Android emulator is anomalous. Rationale: The article explicitly names the 'Genymobile Android emulator' as the group's MFA-attack tool; Genymotion installs under \Genymobile\Genymotion\ with binaries genymotion.exe/gmtool.exe/genyshell.exe and the Genymobile company string, giving a concrete file-path anchor. Confidence is Low because the Genymotion-to-Scattered-Spider link is thinly second-sourced beyond the article/DOJ complaint — deploy as a hunt, scoped away from dev/QA fleets. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genymotion.com/product-desktop/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1621 T1098.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile app developers or QA engineers legitimately running Genymotion for Android testing
  • Security researchers/malware analysts using Genymotion in a sandbox VM
  • IT provisioning a new mobile-dev workstation and installing the emulator suite
  • A shared analysis host where Genymotion is an approved tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the AccountName/DeviceName belongs to a mobile-dev/QA role or approved analysis host; if the user is finance/HR/helpdesk/exec, treat as suspicious. Check install time and who initiated it. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, capture the emulator's ADB/session artifacts, and review the associated account for recent MFA-registration events (pivot to UC1). 3) Hunt: correlate emulator runtime with Entra 'User registered security info' events from that host's IP, and search for adjacent remote-access tooling (AnyDesk/ScreenConnect) commonly staged by the group.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FolderPath has @"\Genymobile\" or FolderPath has @"\Genymotion\")
    or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Genymobile"
    or FileName in~ ("genymotion.exe","gmtool.exe","genyshell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\Genymobile\" or NewProcessName has @"\Genymotion\"
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\genymotion.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\gmtool.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\genyshell.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MFA fatigue / push-bombing Actions on Objectives High
Many MFA pushes to same user in short window — suggests adversary attempting approval-fatigue.
ATT&CKT1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication AADSignInEventsBeta
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode in (50074, 50076, 50158, 50125, 50097)
| extend MfaPrompt = AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| where MfaPrompt
| summarize attempts = count(), distinct_ips = dcount(IPAddress)
    by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where attempts > 10
| order by attempts desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType == 50158        // MFA Challenge required / failed
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs       = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Attempts > 3               // tune to baseline
| order by Attempts desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="failure" AND Authentication.signature="*MFA*"
    by _time span=5m, Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count > 10
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="failure" AND Authentication.signature="*MFA*"
    by _time span=5m, Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count > 10

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.

CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"

| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")

    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

| order by files desc

DeviceEvents

FortiBleed Credential Theft Linked to INC and Lynx Ransomware Operations

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 17 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The recently discovered financially-motivated FortiBleed campaign has been attributed to INC and Lynx ransomware operations, indicating that the verified, stolen credentials were intended for follow-on intrusions. "An operator tied to FortiBleed's infrastructure was found actively working negotiation panels for both groups, tying mass FortiGate credential theft directly to ransomware deployment

FortiClient EMS exposed to CVE-2026-35616 (EKZ Infostealer delivery vector) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed endpoints/servers running FortiClient EMS versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-35616, the pre-auth API bypass eSentire/Arctic Wolf observed being exploited to push the EKZ infostealer disguised as a Fortinet patch. This is the initial-access exposure the whole FortiBleed follow-on chain depends on. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE-2026-35616 id and the exact affected FortiClient EMS builds (7.4.5/7.4.6, fixed 7.4.7) confirmed by Arctic Wolf and Fortinet's advisory — a precise exposure hunt rather than a generic 'outdated software' sweep. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-forticlient-ems-flaw-to-push-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Isolated/segmented lab EMS servers intentionally kept on 7.4.5 for regression testing
  • Vulnerability shows in TVM but the device is already scheduled in this patch cycle (accepted risk)
  • Third-party MSP-managed FortiClient EMS the org does not directly patch
  • TVM version parsing lag right after a 7.4.7 upgrade until next scan completes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the EMS host is internet-reachable and the API port is exposed; check whether the 7.4.7+ patch has actually applied. 2) Contain: restrict EMS API/console to management IPs, force-patch to 7.4.7 or later, and rotate any admin creds used on the appliance. 3) Hunt: on every endpoint managed by that EMS, pivot to UC 'EKZ delivered as fake Fortinet update' and the EKZ hash/browser-theft UCs to rule out downstream deployment.

    or (SoftwareName has "forticlient" and SoftwareName has "ems" and SoftwareVersion in ("7.4.5","7.4.6"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-35616"
    or (SoftwareName has "forticlient" and SoftwareName has "ems" and SoftwareVersion in ("7.4.5","7.4.6"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
FortiBleed / EKZ Infostealer known-bad file hashes on endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on execution or file-write of any of the SOCRadar/eSentire-reported FortiBleed & EKZ payload hashes across process and file telemetry. Direct IOC match for the malware set tied to the FortiGate credential-theft-to-ransomware chain. Rationale: Direct match on the five SHA256, one SHA1 and one MD5 payload hashes carried in the article's IOC set; hash matches are inherently high-fidelity and this campaign's payloads were reported by SOCRadar and eSentire. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-inc-lynx-ransomware-link/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst/reverse-engineering VM where the sample was intentionally detonated
  • EDR or AV quarantine copy retaining the original hash in a vault path
  • Threat-intel sandbox/detonation appliance ingesting the sample
  • Purple-team exercise replaying the IOC set for control validation
Suppression filter
// Defender: exclude known detonation/analysis hosts
| where DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARE-LAB01","SANDBOX-VM01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is not an analyst/sandbox host; capture full path, signer, and parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the device in Defender/Falcon, block the hashes org-wide, and preserve the binary for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot the affected host through the browser-credential-theft and C2-egress UCs, and check whether the parent was a FortiClient EMS agent (fake-update delivery).

EKZ payload delivered as fake Fortinet update: FortiClient agent spawning script host AIDelivery Medium
Detects a FortiClient/FortiClient EMS agent process spawning a script interpreter (PowerShell/cmd/wscript etc.) — the behaviour Arctic Wolf described where the EMS exploit pushes the EKZ stealer to managed endpoints disguised as a Fortinet endpoint update and silently runs it via PowerShell. Legitimate FortiClient components almost never spawn script hosts. Rationale: Anchors on real FortiClient agent process names as the parent (FcmDaemon.exe etc.) spawning a script host — the exact 'fake Fortinet update silently run via PowerShell' delivery Arctic Wolf documented; deliberately does not exclude machine/SYSTEM accounts because FortiClient runs as SYSTEM. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-forticlient-ems-flaw-to-push-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FortiClient EMS deployment package that runs a vendor PowerShell post-install script
  • IT-authored FortiClient install/repair wrapper that shells out to cmd.exe
  • Diagnostic/log-collection tooling invoked by a FortiClient support case
  • Endpoint management script legitimately pushed through EMS during a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FortiClientSetup","install","repair") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vendor","C:\\Program Files\\Fortinet"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line — legitimate FortiClient post-install scripts are signed and reference vendor paths; a download-cradle, hidden window, or exe in a temp path is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the child hash, and freeze further EMS deployments until the EMS server is confirmed patched (CVE-2026-35616). 3) Hunt: sweep all EMS-managed endpoints for the same parent-child pair within the deployment window and pivot to the EKZ hash and browser-theft UCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("FcmDaemon.exe","FortiClient.exe","FortiESNAC.exe","FortiSSLVPNdaemon.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("FcmDaemon.exe","FortiClient.exe","FortiESNAC.exe","FortiSSLVPNdaemon.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EKZ Infostealer access to Chromium/Firefox credential stores by non-browser process AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a non-browser process opening Chrome/Edge 'Login Data' and 'Local State' (the AES key file EKZ needs to bypass Chrome encrypted-password storage) or Firefox 'logins.json'/'key4.db'. This is the core credential-access behaviour of the EKZ infostealer named by eSentire/Arctic Wolf. Rationale: Targets the exact browser artifact filenames EKZ needs — including 'Local State', the file required to decrypt Chrome's app-bound/DPAPI password key that the article's write-ups say EKZ bypasses — accessed by a process that isn't the browser itself. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/29/forticlient-ems-vulnerability-infostealer/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup agent (Veeam/Acronis) reading profile folders including browser data
  • Enterprise browser-migration or profile-sync tooling
  • Endpoint DLP/AV engine scanning the user profile
  • Legitimate password manager import utility reading logins.json/Login Data
  • msedgewebview2 or an Electron app embedding a Chromium profile
Suppression filter
// exclude sanctioned backup/DLP agents
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.exe","acronisagent.exe","mpcmdrun.exe","dlpagent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process and its signer/path — a temp-path or unsigned binary reading Login Data + Local State together is high-confidence theft. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset the affected user's browser-saved and SSO credentials plus session cookies (MFA-protected accounts included, since EKZ steals cookies). 3) Hunt: correlate to outbound egress from the same process (C2-egress UC) and check for the EKZ payload hashes on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data")
    or FolderPath has_any ("User Data","Profiles")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","msedgewebview2.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","msedgewebview2.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Store (EKZ Infostealer)
id: 4a8f2b6d-73c1-4e59-b0a7-9c2e1f5d380b
description: Detects a non-browser process opening Chromium/Firefox credential and encryption-key files, consistent with EKZ infostealer credential theft.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fortibleed-credential-theft-linked-to.html
  - https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1539
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - 'Login Data'
      - 'Local State'
      - 'key4.db'

  filter_browsers:

      - 'opera.exe'

  condition: selection and not filter_browsers
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*Login?Data OR *Local?State OR *key4.db OR *logins.json OR *cookies.sqlite OR *Web?Data) -@Image:(*chrome.exe OR *msedge.exe OR *firefox.exe OR *brave.exe OR *opera.exe OR *vivaldi.exe OR *msedgewebview2.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/(Login Data|Local State|key4\.db|logins\.json|cookies\.sqlite|Web Data)$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera|vivaldi|msedgewebview2)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("Login Data","Local State","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("Login Data","Local State","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Egress to FortiBleed C2 infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host or firewall connection to the three FortiBleed infrastructure IPs reported alongside the campaign, catching EKZ credential exfiltration and INC/Lynx C2. Two of the three are Tor exit nodes, so process/context is required to keep this high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the three campaign IPs from the article's IOC set across endpoint (Defender/Falcon/Sysmon) and firewall (CommonSecurityLog, well-suited since victims run FortiGate) telemetry; the projected process/user context is what turns the two Tor-exit IPs from noise into an actionable exfil signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-inc-lynx-ransomware-link/ • https://www.securityweek.com/russian-initial-access-broker-behind-fortibleed-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • 185.220.101.15 and 192.42.116.14 fall in known Tor exit ranges — benign Tor Browser use by a researcher or privacy-conscious user
  • Threat-intel enrichment box actively probing the IP
  • Security scanner/pentest tooling connecting to the infrastructure during authorized testing
  • Shared NAT egress causing a benign internal host to appear as the source
Suppression filter
// Focus egress on non-browser initiators to strip benign Tor use
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the initiating process — powershell.exe or an unsigned binary reaching these IPs (especially 83.138.53.110) is high-confidence exfil; a browser hitting a Tor IP is likely benign Tor use. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at the firewall/EDR, isolate the source host, and rotate credentials that may have been exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: sweep firewall logs for other internal hosts touching the same IPs and pivot the source host through the EKZ hash and browser-credential-theft UCs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("83.138.53.110","185.220.101.15","192.42.116.14")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("83.138.53.110","185.220.101.15","192.42.116.14")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

            - '\Cookies'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

let BadHashes = dynamic(["0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081"]);

New ChocoPoC RAT Targets Vulnerability Researchers via Fake PoC Exploit Repos

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers are hiding a data-stealing trojan inside fake exploit code aimed at the people who hunt bugs for a living. The malware, called ChocoPoC, travels in Python proof-of-concept (PoC) repositories on GitHub that claim to exploit hot new CVEs. Run one, and it quietly lifts your saved passwords, browser cookies, and files, then hands the attacker a shell on your machine.&nbsp;YesWeHack and
