Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ChocoPoC gradient native extension loaded into Python interpreter (detonation) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New ChocoPoC RAT Targets Vulnerability Researchers via Fake PoC Exploit Repos
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ChocoPoC malicious PyPI dependency dropped into site-packages (skytext/frint + gradient native ext) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Python-initiated Mapbox dead-drop C2 over DNS-over-HTTPS (ChocoPoC control channel) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Python process reading browser credential stores (ChocoPoC stealer collection) · [LLM] ChocoPoC bulk exfiltration to dedicated server 91.132.163.78 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ChocoPoC malicious PyPI dependency dropped into site-packages (skytext/frint + gradient native ext) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ChocoPoC delivery step: pip/python writing the malicious dependency chain (frint→skytext, or the older slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) and its compiled loader gradient.pyd/gradient.so into a Python site-packages directory. This is the on-disk fingerprint of a trojanized PoC repo's requirements being installed. Rationale: Anchors on second-sourced concrete artifacts: package names frint/skytext (and predecessor slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) plus the compiled loader gradient.pyd/gradient.so, scoped to site-packages and a pip/python writer — a shape no benign install matches. Corroborated by BleepingComputer's Sekoia writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign PyPI package coincidentally shipping a compiled module named gradient.pyd/gradient.so (some ML libs use 'gradient' module names)
  • A dev intentionally testing/analyzing the malware in a sandbox after this report
  • Internal mirror re-hosting a package folder literally named skytext/frint for research
  • Security researcher extracting the sample into a project workspace under site-packages
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\site-packages\\numpy","\\site-packages\\torch","\\site-packages\\sklearn") and FileName == "gradient.pyd")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full FolderPath and SHA256 of gradient.pyd/.so and the parent pip/python command line; confirm the package name is exactly frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt and whether a PoC repo (EXPLOIT_POC.py) exists on the host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the python interpreter that loaded the module, and quarantine the site-packages folder; treat any credentials used on that host (SSH keys, cloud tokens, client creds) as compromised. 3) HUNT: Pivot to outbound connections to 91.132.163.78 and python→mapbox.com traffic from the same DeviceId, and sweep the org for the same package folders/hashes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")
    or (FolderPath has "site-packages" and FolderPath has_any ("skytext","frint","slogsec","logcrypt"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pip","python")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")
    or (TargetFilePath has "site-packages" and TargetFilePath has_any ("skytext","frint","slogsec","logcrypt"))
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChocoPoC Malicious PyPI Package Artifact Written to site-packages
id: 5f3a2b1c-8d4e-4a6f-9b2c-1e7d3f4a5b6c
description: Detects the ChocoPoC delivery chain writing gradient.pyd/gradient.so or the skytext/frint/slogsec/logcrypt package folders into a Python site-packages directory.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_artifact:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\gradient.pyd'
      - '/gradient.so'
  selection_pkg:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\skytext\'
      - '/skytext/'
      - '\frint\'
      - '/frint/'
      - '\slogsec\'
      - '/slogsec/'
      - 'logcrypt'
  condition: selection_artifact or selection_pkg
falsepositives:
  - Unrelated packages that legitimately ship a module named gradient
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\gradient.pyd OR *\\gradient.so OR *\\skytext\\* OR *\\frint\\* OR *\\slogsec\\*) OR @TargetFilename:(*/gradient.so OR */skytext/* OR */frint/*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(gradient\.(pyd|so)|[\\\/](skytext|frint|slogsec|logcrypt)[\\\/])/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(pip|python)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so") OR Filesystem.file_path IN ("*site-packages*skytext*","*site-packages*frint*","*site-packages*slogsec*","*site-packages*logcrypt*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so") OR Filesystem.file_path IN ("*site-packages*skytext*","*site-packages*frint*","*site-packages*slogsec*","*site-packages*logcrypt*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
ChocoPoC gradient native extension loaded into Python interpreter (detonation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the execution moment: the malicious compiled extension gradient.pyd (Windows) / gradient.so (Linux) being loaded by a python/pip process. This confirms the trojanized dependency actually ran, not just installed, and fires only when the PoC context triggers the loader. Rationale: gradient.pyd/gradient.so loaded specifically inside a python interpreter is the unique detonation signature described (the loader wakes only when the PoC is present) — far higher fidelity than the file drop because it proves execution. Splunk left empty as CIM has no image-load datamodel (use raw Sysmon EventCode=7); Falcon left empty as FDR's provided schema exposes no generic module-load event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1129
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst intentionally detonating the sample in a monitored VM post-report
  • A wholly unrelated Python C-extension named gradient.pyd shipped by a legitimate package being imported
  • Automated dependency-scanning tooling that imports packages to introspect them
  • Re-runs of the same PoC during IR reproduction on an already-flagged host
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the loading python process tree, working directory, and whether EXPLOIT_POC.py or a cloned CVE PoC repo is present; hash gradient.pyd/.so and check against the Sekoia report IOCs. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, suspend/kill the python process, block outbound to 91.132.163.78 and mapbox.com from that host. 3) HUNT: Look for immediate follow-on — python spawning shells, browser credential-store access, and DoH/mapbox C2 beacons on the same DeviceId.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","pip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| where EventData has_any ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")
| where EventData has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, RenderedDescription
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChocoPoC gradient Native Extension Loaded by Python
id: 7a1b2c3d-4e5f-4061-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b
description: Detects load of the ChocoPoC compiled loader gradient.pyd/gradient.so into a python or pip process.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.t1129
logsource:
  category: image_load
detection:
  selection_module:
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\gradient.pyd'
      - '/gradient.so'
  selection_host:
    Image|contains: 'python'
  condition: selection_module and selection_host
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 @ImageLoaded:(*\\gradient.pyd OR */gradient.so) @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR */python OR */python3)
Python process reading browser credential stores (ChocoPoC stealer collection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts ChocoPoC's credential-theft stage: a python-family process (not the browser itself) touching Chrome/Brave/Edge/Firefox credential and cookie databases (Login Data, Cookies, key4.db, logins.json). Browsers read their own stores; a python reader is the anomaly. Rationale: Article states ChocoPoC lifts saved passwords/cookies/autofill/history from Chrome, Brave, Edge and Firefox; the high-fidelity twist is that the reader is the python interpreter (from the malicious dependency), not the browser. Datadog left empty because standard Sysmon/auditd shipping doesn't capture file-open/read of these DBs without custom watch rules; Falcon FileOpenInfo carries the read directly. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate python browser-automation frameworks (Selenium profile handling, playwright) touching profile files
  • DFIR/forensics tooling written in python parsing browser artifacts on an analyst workstation
  • Backup or profile-migration scripts copying browser profiles
  • Password-manager import utilities implemented in python
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("selenium","playwright","browser_history","forensic")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the python process's parent chain and whether gradient.pyd/.so is loaded by it; confirm the target profile belongs to a real user vs a service. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, kill the python process, and force-rotate the user's browser-saved credentials, session cookies, and any SSO tokens; invalidate active web sessions. 3) HUNT: Correlate with subsequent exfil to 91.132.163.78 or mapbox C2 from the same host, and check for shell-history/network-config file reads by the same process.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite")
    or FolderPath has_any ("logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "python"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType,
          FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChocoPoC bulk exfiltration to dedicated server 91.132.163.78 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the large-upload channel: any host connecting outbound to the ChocoPoC exfiltration server 91.132.163.78, which the malware uses for larger uploads separate from its Mapbox control channel. Straight IOC match with process attribution projected for triage. Rationale: Direct IOC: the article names 91.132.163.78 as the dedicated server for larger uploads. Confidence set to Medium and flagged because this IP is single-sourced (only the original article; not confirmed in the corroborating BleepingComputer/Sekoia summary) — the exact-IP match keeps fidelity high but analysts should validate liveness before hard-blocking. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The IP being reassigned to a benign hosting tenant after takedown (stale IOC)
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning tooling in the SOC deliberately probing the IP
  • Shared-hosting neighbor on the same address serving unrelated legitimate content
  • Researcher sandbox traffic during controlled detonation
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process (expect python) and byte volume; confirm the connection is not from a sanctioned scanner. 2) CONTAIN: Block 91.132.163.78 at egress, isolate the host, and preserve netflow/pcap for the session to scope what was uploaded. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same DeviceId for gradient.pyd/.so loads, browser-credential access, and mapbox.com C2; sweep all hosts for any prior connection to the IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "91.132.163.78"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "91.132.163.78"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkBytes, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python-initiated Mapbox dead-drop C2 over DNS-over-HTTPS (ChocoPoC control channel) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts ChocoPoC's stealthy control channel: a python-family process resolving/contacting Mapbox (dead-drop dataset) or public DoH resolvers, used with domain-fronting to disguise C2 as ordinary Mapbox API traffic. Hunting-tier because Mapbox/DoH are legitimate services — the anomaly is a python interpreter driving them. Rationale: Article and Sekoia summary describe C2 orders read from a Mapbox dataset dead-drop, resolved over DNS-over-HTTPS with domain-fronting. Detection keys on the distinctive combination of a python interpreter driving Mapbox and/or DoH-resolver traffic. Sigma omitted: this is a cross-field process+network correlation not a single-event shape; Sentinel ImNetworkSession lacks reliable per-process attribution so it flags mapbox/DoH destinations for analyst pivoting rather than auto-alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1090.004 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate python GIS/mapping apps or notebooks using the Mapbox API
  • python tooling configured to use DoH resolvers for privacy (e.g. requests-doh, dnspython over HTTPS)
  • CI/build agents in python pulling map tiles or geocoding data
  • Researcher scripts that legitimately query Mapbox datasets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("geocode","tile","folium","geopandas","mapbox_sdk")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the host has any legitimate mapping/GIS use; inspect the python process for gradient.pyd/.so load and check the Mapbox dataset/URL path being polled. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, isolate the host, kill the python process, and block the specific Mapbox dataset endpoint plus 91.132.163.78 at egress. 3) HUNT: Look for the delivery artifacts (skytext/frint/gradient) and browser-credential access on the same host; review DoH usage org-wide for other python-driven beacons.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

SharePoint/Triofox LFI probing for win.ini & web.config (Storm-2603 initial access) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to internet-facing SharePoint/Gladinet Triofox endpoints that retrieve win.ini or web.config (including the corroborated /storage/t.dn LFI endpoint used to steal the ASP.NET machineKey). This is the article's stated initial-access probe preceding CVE-2025-11371 / CVE-2026-45659 exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact LFI artifacts (win.ini, web.config) plus the second-source Huntress-confirmed /storage/t.dn and UploadDownloadProxy Triofox endpoints; retrieval of web.config yields the machineKey enabling ViewState RCE, so a served (status<400) hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/gladinet-centrestack-triofox-local-file-inclusion-flaw • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/from-lfi-to-rce-active-exploitation.html • https://securityaffairs.com/183259/hacking/cve-2025-11371-unpatched-zero-day-in-gladinet-centrestack-triofox-under-attack.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing for LFI as part of authorized assessments
  • Legitimate SharePoint health-check tooling reading web.config over HTTP
  • Backup/config-management agents fetching web.config via web endpoints
  • Security researchers or red-team engagements hitting /storage/t.dn
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "nmap", "masscan", "Nuclei") and cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8")   // exclude sanctioned scanners / internal ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP and confirm whether web.config/machineKey content was actually returned (status 200 + response size); check if the source IP is an internal scanner or external. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter and, if a served web.config is confirmed, rotate the SharePoint/Triofox ASP.NET machineKey and force IIS recycle to invalidate forged ViewState. 3) Hunt: on the affected server look for follow-on ViewState deserialization POSTs, w3wp.exe spawning cmd/powershell, and any Velociraptor or remote-access-tool execution within the following hours.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem has_any ("win.ini", "web.config", "t.dn") or csUriQuery has_any ("win.ini", "web.config")
| where scStatus < 400   // only successful/served retrievals of the sensitive file
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Velociraptor DFIR agent executed as attacker tooling (Storm-2603 execution) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution or service install of the Velociraptor DFIR binary on hosts that are not sanctioned incident-response endpoints. The article states Storm-2603 deployed Velociraptor with SYSTEM privileges to blend malicious activity with trusted admin behaviour. Rationale: Velociraptor is named explicitly in the article as the DFIR tool Storm-2603 abused; the binary name, client artifact strings, and SYSTEM-integrity execution are distinctive and rare outside sanctioned IR, giving low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/velociraptor-incident-response-tool-abused-for-remote-access • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/
ATT&CKT1105 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Your own DFIR/IR team legitimately deploying Velociraptor during an investigation
  • MSSP or Sophos/Huntress-managed Velociraptor agent as a sanctioned monitoring tool
  • Security lab / detection-engineering testing of Velociraptor
  • Threat-hunting exercises running the binary on a jump-host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("IR-JUMPHOST01", "DFIR-TOOLS01")   // populate with sanctioned IR endpoints
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a sanctioned IR endpoint and whether your team deployed Velociraptor; inspect the config/frontend URL in the command line to see where it reports (attacker C2 vs internal). 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host, kill the Velociraptor process/service, and capture the config file for the C2 address. 3) Hunt: pivot on the config's frontend domain across DeviceNetworkEvents, and look for co-occurring new admin accounts, cloudflared tunnels, and NSecKrnl.sys driver drops on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "velociraptor.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("velociraptor", "artifact_collector", "Velociraptor.Client", "--config", "frontend")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Velociraptor"
// exclude sanctioned DFIR jump-hosts by DeviceName if you have them
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\velociraptor.exe" or CommandLine has_any ("velociraptor", "artifact_collector", "Velociraptor.Client")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

NSecKrnl.sys vulnerable driver drop/install (Storm-2603 BYOVD EDR tampering) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation on disk or service installation of the vulnerable NSecKrnl.sys driver, which the article states was used as a BYOVD conduit to tamper with endpoint protection and reduce visibility. Any appearance of this driver name is high-signal. Rationale: NSecKrnl.sys is the exact vulnerable driver named in the article as the BYOVD conduit for EDR tampering; a fixed, uncommon driver filename makes any hit essentially a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188359/unpatched-sharepoint-servers-opened-the-door-to-multiple-attackers-microsoft-finds.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate product that genuinely ships a driver literally named NSecKrnl.sys (verify vendor signature and path)
  • Security-research/malware-analysis sandbox intentionally detonating the BYOVD sample
  • Restore of a forensic image that contains the artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path, SHA256 and signer of NSecKrnl.sys and the process that wrote it (InitiatingProcessFileName); check whether a matching kernel service was registered (7045). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, block the driver hash org-wide, and treat EDR telemetry from that host as untrusted (assume tampering) — validate the sensor is still reporting. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same driver hash/name and service, and correlate with Velociraptor execution, new admin accounts, and EDR sensor-stop/config-change events around the same timestamp.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "NSecKrnl.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceFileName has "NSecKrnl" or ServiceName has "NSecKrnl"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker remote-access channels: cloudflared tunnel, Zoho Assist, VS Code SSH tunnel AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts execution of the three specific redundant remote-access channels the article attributes to Storm-2603 for persistent C2: Cloudflare tunneling (cloudflared tunnel), Zoho Assist agents, and Visual Studio Code SSH/remote tunnels. Targets server assets where these tools are not normally present. Rationale: The three channels (Cloudflare tunneling, Zoho Assist, VS Code SSH) are named verbatim in the article and confirmed by second sources; scoping cloudflared/code to the 'tunnel' subcommand keeps the signal on the actual tunnel behaviour rather than benign launches. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/ • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/
ATT&CKT1572 T1219 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately running 'code tunnel' (VS Code Remote Tunnels) on workstations
  • IT support using Zoho Assist as a sanctioned remote-support tool
  • Sanctioned Cloudflare Tunnel deployment for internal app publishing
  • CI/CD or dev machines with cloudflared for local testing
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "DEV" and DeviceName !has "WKS"   // reduce developer-workstation noise; keep server/DC assets in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the host is a server/DC (high suspicion) vs a developer workstation, and inspect the tunnel target — cloudflared config/token, Zoho session ID, or VS Code tunnel name — for external ownership. 2) Contain: on server/infrastructure assets, kill the process and any associated service, and block the tunnel egress domains (*.trycloudflare.com, *.cloudflare.com tunnels, zoho assist domains) from that host. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/account with Velociraptor, NSecKrnl.sys, and new admin-account creation, and check whether the same remote-access tooling appears on a second organization/host (article notes lateral movement into a second org).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
    or FileName in~ ("ZA_Access.exe", "ZA_Connect.exe", "ZMAgent.exe", "ZohoMeeting.exe", "ZohoURS.exe")
    or (FileName =~ "code.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\cloudflared.exe" and CommandLine has "tunnel")
    or NewProcessName has_any ("ZA_Access.exe", "ZA_Connect.exe", "ZMAgent.exe", "ZohoMeeting.exe", "ZohoURS.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\code.exe" and CommandLine has "tunnel")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Redundant Remote-Access Tunnels (cloudflared / Zoho Assist / VS Code SSH)

New local/domain admin account creation and privileged-group grant (Storm-2603 persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts creation of new accounts followed by (or directly) their addition to Administrators / Domain Admins / Enterprise Admins, and command-line net user/group /add of admin members. The article states Storm-2603 escalated by creating new local and domain administrator accounts. Rationale: Directly targets the article's 'created new local and domain administrator accounts' behaviour via both auth telemetry (4728/4732 to well-known admin SID S-1-5-32-544) and the net.exe /add command line, which is the concrete on-host method. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188359/unpatched-sharepoint-servers-opened-the-door-to-multiple-attackers-microsoft-finds.html
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1136.002 T1078.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IT provisioning of new admin accounts during onboarding/imaging
  • Identity-management/PAM automation adding accounts to privileged groups
  • Legitimate helpdesk scripts using net localgroup administrators /add
  • Domain migration or M&A activity creating admin accounts in bulk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-idm", "svc-provisioning") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pam_agent.exe")   // exclude sanctioned provisioning identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the actor (SubjectUserName/InitiatingProcessAccountName) and the created account; confirm whether a change ticket exists and whether the actor is itself a recently-created or compromised account. 2) Contain: disable the newly created account, remove it from privileged groups, and force a password reset on the actor account; on a DC, verify replication of the malicious group change is reversed. 3) Hunt: correlate the new account's first logons across hosts (lateral movement to a second org per the article), and check for co-occurring Velociraptor, cloudflared/Zoho/VS Code tunnels, and NSecKrnl.sys on the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.exe", "net1.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/add"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "user") or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("localgroup", "group") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("administrators", "domain admins", "enterprise admins"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4728, 4732)   // member added to global (4728) / local (4732) security-enabled group
| where TargetSid == "S-1-5-32-544" or TargetUserName in~ ("Administrators", "Domain Admins", "Enterprise Admins")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Actor = SubjectUserName, AddedMember = MemberName, Group = TargetUserName, EventID
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")

| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2025-11371")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2025-11371")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiBleed 'adminin' backdoor local account creation and logon AIInstallation High
Hunts creation and subsequent use of a local account named 'adminin' — the exact backdoor username SOCRadar found planted on FortiBleed-compromised systems for persistent access. Fires on both the account-creation command and any logon by that account. Rationale: Anchored on the exact backdoor username 'adminin' from the article's code block; SOCRadar/SecurityWeek independently confirm the operators 'make backdoor users' on compromised FortiBleed hosts, making this a near-zero-FP named-account detection. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-fortinet-firewalls-compromised/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/active-fortibleed-campaign-impacting-fortinet-devices-across-194-countries/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An organization legitimately standardizes admin service accounts on a similar naming scheme (e.g. 'adminintl' truncated in a script)
  • Red-team / purple-team exercise recreating the FortiBleed backdoor for detection validation
  • IT provisioning template that reuses a generic bootstrap account name
  • Migration tooling that recreates local accounts during OS re-imaging
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceProcessEvents/4720 record — who (InitiatingProcessAccountName) created 'adminin', from what parent process, and whether it was added to Administrators/Remote Desktop groups. Correlate the logon RemoteIP against known-good admin subnets. 2) Contain: disable/delete the 'adminin' account, force-reset any admin credentials on the host, and isolate the device from the network if it is an internet-facing appliance mgmt host. 3) Hunt: sweep every host and FortiGate for the same account name, look for outbound connections to unfamiliar hosting IPs, and check for downloaded FortiGate config files and the FortigateSniffer tool.
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "adminin"
  | where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "user" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/add","-add"))
       or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-LocalUser","Add-LocalGroupMember"))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="LocalAccountCreated", Account="adminin", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
 (DeviceLogonEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where AccountName =~ "adminin"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="BackdoorAccountLogon", Account=AccountName, Detail=strcat("LogonType=", tostring(LogonType), " RemoteIP=", RemoteIP), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountDomain)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID in (4720,4732,4728,4726) and TargetUserName =~ "adminin")
     or (EventID == 4624 and TargetUserName =~ "adminin")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Activity, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, IpAddress, LogonType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FortiBleed 'adminin' Backdoor Local Account Creation
id: 3f2a1c94-8d0e-4b7a-9a21-5c6e2f0b71aa
description: Detects creation of a local account named 'adminin', the backdoor username SOCRadar attributed to the FortiBleed credential-theft operation linked to INC/Lynx ransomware.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fortibleed-credential-theft-campaign-linked-to-lynx-ransomware/
  - https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-fortinet-firewalls-compromised/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:

  - attack.t1136.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\net1.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'user'
      - 'adminin'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/add'
      - '-add'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd
level: high
source:windows.security (@EventID:4720 OR @EventID:4624 OR @EventID:4732 OR @EventID:4726) @TargetUserName:(adminin OR Adminin OR ADMININ)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/\bnet1?\s+user\s+adminin\b.*(\/add|-add)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count(as=execCount))
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")) Processes.process="*adminin*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(user\s+adminin.*(/add|-add)|New-LocalUser.*adminin|Add-LocalGroupMember.*adminin)") | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")) Processes.process="*adminin*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(user\s+adminin.*(/add|-add)|New-LocalUser.*adminin|Add-LocalGroupMember.*adminin)") | sort - lastTime
Credential-stuffing burst culminating in success against FortiGate SSL-VPN / SSO AIExploitation Medium
Detects the FortiBleed reuse pattern: many failed authentications from a single source IP across multiple usernames followed by at least one success — the harvested/cracked Fortinet credentials being stuffed against SSL-VPN gateways and reused against Entra SSO. Rationale: The article and multiple corroborating sources state credential stuffing is the PRIMARY collection/reuse mechanism of FortiBleed; the one-IP/many-users/many-fails-then-success shape against FortiGate SSL-VPN and Entra SSO is the article-specific signature of stolen-credential reuse, not a generic brute-force template. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/security-alert-fortibleed-fortinet-vpn-credentials-firewall-exposed
ATT&CKT1110.004 T1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate NAT/VPN concentrator egressing many users behind one public IP triggering the distinct-user threshold
  • Misconfigured mobile client or expired-password loop generating repeated failures then a success after reset
  • Security scanner / authenticated vulnerability scan hitting the VPN portal
  • SSO migration event causing bulk re-authentication from a proxy IP
Suppression filter
// exclude known corporate egress / NAT gateways before alerting:
| where SourceIP !in ("") // populate with your published corporate egress IPs; keep external-only IPs in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not a corporate NAT gateway; enumerate which usernames succeeded and whether MFA was satisfied. 2) Contain: force password reset + session revocation on every successfully-authenticated account from that IP, block the source IP at the FortiGate and IdP, and enforce MFA on SSL-VPN if absent. 3) Hunt: check whether any of the compromised accounts have Fortinet-managed credentials matching the FortiBleed dumps, review those accounts for 'adminin' creation, config downloads, and lateral movement toward file servers/backup hosts.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| summarize Failures = countif(ErrorCode != 0), Successes = countif(ErrorCode == 0), DistinctUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleApps = make_set(Application, 5) by IPAddress
| where DistinctUsers >= 10 and Failures >= 20 and Successes >= 1   // one IP, 10+ users, 20+ fails, >=1 success = stuffing signature
| order by Failures desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl-login","sslvpn","vpn","login") or Message has_any ("SSL VPN","login")
| extend Outcome = tolower(coalesce(EventOutcome, DeviceAction, Message))
| summarize Failures = countif(Outcome has_any ("fail","deny","error")), Successes = countif(Outcome has_any ("success","accept","ok","tunnel-up")), DistinctUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where DistinctUsers >= 10 and Failures >= 20 and Successes >= 1
| order by Failures desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:50126
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where (Authentication.app="fortigate" OR Authentication.app="*ssl*vpn*" OR Authentication.app="*vpn*") by Authentication.src Authentication.action Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes dc(user) as user_count values(user) as users by src | where failures >= 20 AND successes >= 1 AND user_count >= 10 | sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where (Authentication.app="fortigate" OR Authentication.app="*ssl*vpn*" OR Authentication.app="*vpn*") by Authentication.src Authentication.action Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes dc(user) as user_count values(user) as users by src | where failures >= 20 AND successes >= 1 AND user_count >= 10 | sort - failures
FortiGate admin login and configuration download from external IP AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed initial-access footprint on edge devices: administrative authentication to a FortiGate from a public/Internet source IP paired with configuration backup/download activity — the exact behaviour that produced the exposed cache of FortiGate config files. Rationale: Anchored on the article's 'downloaded FortiGate configuration files' collection artifact plus the mass edge-device compromise; scoping FortiGate config-download/admin-login to a non-private (external) source IP flags attacker administrative access rather than internal management. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty as FortiGate appliance logs do not ship to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-fortinet-firewalls-compromised/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186790/fortibleed-campaign-exposes-75000-fortinet-firewalls-worldwide.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1602.002 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote administrator managing the FortiGate over the public interface from a home/ISP IP
  • MSP/outsourced NOC performing scheduled configuration backups from their own cloud IP
  • Vendor support session downloading config for troubleshooting
  • Monitoring tool pulling config snapshots via API from an external SaaS source
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("") // populate with approved external management source IPs (MSP/NOC/admin home IPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the admin account and source IP; verify against the approved management-IP allowlist and change-management tickets for a config backup at that time. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable/rotate the admin credential, restrict the mgmt interface to trusted IPs / VPN only, and pull the current config to diff against baseline for rogue admins ('adminin'), added VPN users, or a packet-sniffer/FortigateSniffer artifact. 3) Hunt: review VPN auth logs for stuffing bursts, check for outbound connections to unfamiliar hosting IPs, and correlate the org against INC/Lynx leak-site listings.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("Configuration is downloaded","config backup","backup config","Admin login successful","login successful") or Activity has_any ("download","backup","admin-login")
| extend SrcIP = SourceIP
| where isnotempty(SrcIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName = DeviceExternalID, SrcIP, DestinationHostName, SourceUserName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  • Threat-intel or ASM scanner in your environment probing the flagged IP
  • Security researcher/sandbox traffic to the IP from a lab host
  • Stale IOC firing on historical benign traffic if the address was previously legitimate
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm current reputation of 85.11.187.8 (VT/ThreatFox/passive DNS) and identify the initiating process/user and data volume (bytes out). 2) Contain: block the IP at perimeter/EDR, and if the source is a FortiGate or server staging harvested data, isolate it. 3) Hunt: expand to the wider operator fleet by pivoting on ASN/hosting neighbors, look for config/credential archive uploads, 'adminin' accounts, and any Lynx/INC follow-on activity on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.11.187.8"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP == "85.11.187.8" or SourceIP == "85.11.187.8" | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, SourceUserName),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "85.11.187.8" or SrcIpAddr == "85.11.187.8" | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=85.11.187.8

Lynx/INC ransomware mass file encryption via .lynx extension AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage the FortiBleed access ultimately fed: bulk creation/rename of files with the '.lynx' extension by a single process, the hallmark of Lynx (INC rebrand) ransomware encryption. Corroborated extension across multiple vendor analyses. Rationale: The article explicitly links FortiBleed access to Lynx/INC ransomware impact; Unit42, Nextron, FortiGuard and Rapid7 independently confirm Lynx appends the unique '.lynx' extension and drops README.txt, so bulk '.lynx' writes by one process is a high-fidelity, article-specific impact detection. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/inc-ransomware-rebrand-to-lynx/ • https://www.nextron-systems.com/2024/10/11/in-depth-analysis-of-lynx-ransomware/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/ransomware-roundup-lynx • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/09/12/ransomware-groups-demystified-lynx-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application or dataset that coincidentally uses a '.lynx' file extension (rare; e.g. niche lynx browser cache/config artifacts)
  • Backup/restore of a previously-encrypted dataset re-introducing .lynx files
  • Security team detonating a Lynx sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Renaming utility batch-appending '.lynx' during a controlled DFIR exercise
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and account, confirm whether README.txt ransom notes were dropped in the same directories and whether Volume Shadow Copies were deleted. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host from the network, kill/suspend the encrypting process, and preserve memory and a disk image; check for spread to file servers/backup infrastructure (Veeam/MSSQL/Exchange). 3) Hunt: trace the intrusion back — FortiGate VPN stuffing logins, 'adminin' backdoor accounts, config downloads, and outbound staging to unfamiliar hosting IPs — and cross-reference the org against INC/Lynx leak-site listings; engage IR and preserve keys for possible decryption recovery.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".lynx"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Proc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), ProcCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileCount >= 25   // 25 = mass-encryption burst; lower to 1 for max sensitivity given unique extension
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "lynx" or TargetFileName endswith ".lynx"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Proc = any(ActingProcessName) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount >= 25
| order by FirstSeen desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-24858")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-24858")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-24858")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-24858")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New ChocoPoC malware targets researchers via trojanized PoC exploits

BleepingComputer
2026-07-01 7 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Multiple weaponized proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits on GitHub were found delivering a Python-based remote access trojan (RAT) named ChocoPoC that can execute commands and steal sensitive data in a campaign believed to target cybersecurity researchers. [...]

CVEsCVE-2025-64446 CVE-2025-55182 CVE-2025-14847 CVE-2026-0257 CVE-2026-10520 CVE-2026-50751 CVE-2026-48908
ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1555.003
