Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious ChocoPoC PyPI package install (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) from cloned PoC repo
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Python loading native ChocoPoC extension (.so/.pyd) from skytext/frint package dir
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Python process contacting Mapbox dataset API (ChocoPoC download + exfil channel)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Python/shell reading browser credential & cookie stores (ChocoPoC stealer) · [LLM] Python bulk enumeration of sensitive files (.md/.txt/.db/.sqlite) from PoC context · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Malicious ChocoPoC PyPI package install (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) from cloned PoC repo AIDelivery High
Hunts pip/python installing the named ChocoPoC supply-chain packages 'frint' and its transitive dependency 'skytext' (plus the older 'slogsec' and 'logcrypt.cryptography' variants) into site-packages. This is the delivery step where cloning a trojanized GitHub PoC auto-fetches the malicious dependency chain. Rationale: Uses the four exact PyPI package names Sekoia named (frint, skytext, slogsec, logcrypt.cryptography) written into site/dist-packages by pip/python — these strings do not appear in benign installs; corroborated via Sekoia research and a second BleepingComputer report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate unrelated PyPI package genuinely named 'frint' if one is later published
  • Internal mirror/proxy re-caching these package names for takedown analysis
  • Malware-analysis lab intentionally detonating the sample
  • Security researcher reproducing the Sekoia findings in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--index-url https://pypi.org/simple") and FolderPath has "/analysis-sandbox/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent context — was pip invoked from a freshly cloned GitHub PoC directory (check InitiatingProcessParentFileName=git and the working dir)? Grab the SHA256 of any .so/.pyd under the skytext/frint dirs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python interpreter, and quarantine the site-packages/frint and /skytext directories; block outbound to api.mapbox.com from that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same package names org-wide, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the host reaching Mapbox datasets (UC3) and browser-cred file access (UC4).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/frint/","/skytext/","/slogsec/","/logcrypt","\\frint\\","\\skytext\\","\\slogsec\\","\\logcrypt")
| where FolderPath has "site-packages" or FolderPath has "dist-packages"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/frint/","/skytext/","/slogsec/","/logcrypt","\\frint\\","\\skytext\\","\\slogsec\\","\\logcrypt")
| where TargetFilePath has "site-packages" or TargetFilePath has "dist-packages"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious ChocoPoC PyPI Package Installation

Python loading native ChocoPoC extension (.so/.pyd) from skytext/frint package dir AIInstallation High
Detects the Python interpreter loading a compiled native extension (.so/.pyd) directly from the malicious 'skytext' or 'frint' package directory. Per Sekoia this native extension auto-runs on PoC execution and decrypts embedded Python that stages the downloader — a distinct defense-evasion/unpacking step. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package dirs (skytext/frint) named by Sekoia AND the native-extension file type the article says auto-decrypts the next stage — python loading a .so from a PyPI package dir is normal, but from these named dirs it is the malicious unpacker. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1027 T1140 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate future package named 'frint'/'skytext' shipping a native extension
  • Malware-analysis detonation in a sandbox
  • Researcher reproducing Sekoia's PoC
  • Package name collision on an internal PyPI mirror
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded .so/.pyd and submit to sandbox/VT; confirm the module lives under site-packages/skytext or /frint and was loaded by an interpreter started from a cloned PoC dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the interpreter, quarantine the package dir, and snapshot memory if in-scope (decryption is in-process). 3) Hunt: search the host and org for outbound Mapbox dataset requests (UC3) and browser credential-store access (UC4) that follow this load.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/skytext/","/frint/","\\skytext\\","\\frint\\")
| where FileName endswith ".so" or FileName endswith ".pyd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where FileName endswith ".so" or FileName endswith ".pyd"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python process contacting Mapbox dataset API (ChocoPoC download + exfil channel) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a Python interpreter making HTTP(S)/DNS requests to mapbox.com / api.mapbox.com. Sekoia reports ChocoPoC is retrieved FROM a Mapbox dataset and that Mapbox datasets are abused for data exfiltration — a python process (vs a mapping app or browser) reaching Mapbox is the C2/exfil tell. Rationale: Pairs the exact C2/exfil infrastructure Sekoia named (Mapbox datasets, mapbox.com) with the delivering process class (python) — Mapbox is legitimately called by browsers/mapping SDKs, so scoping to the python interpreter is what makes it a detection rather than noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567.002 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a legitimate Python app that uses the Mapbox SDK/geocoding API
  • Data-science notebook (jupyter kernel = python) pulling map tiles
  • CI job testing a mapping integration
  • Internal GIS tooling written in Python
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("mapbox_sdk","geocoding","folium","mapboxgl") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/opt/gis/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — is the python a known Mapbox-SDK app, or an interpreter launched from a cloned PoC/site-packages context? Pull the Mapbox dataset ID / URL path and request sizes. 2) Contain: block api.mapbox.com egress from the host, isolate if the python has no legitimate Mapbox use, and capture outbound payloads. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (package install) and UC4 (browser cred theft) on the same host/user; check for a secondary HTTP server upload path used for larger files.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where RemoteUrl has "mapbox.com" or RemoteUrl has "api.mapbox.com"
| summarize Connections=count(), BytesContext=make_set(RemotePort,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "mapbox.com"
| summarize Queries=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Python/shell reading browser credential & cookie stores (ChocoPoC stealer) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a Python interpreter or shell touching browser secret stores (Chrome/Edge 'Login Data'/'Cookies'/'Web Data', Firefox logins.json/key4.db/cookies.sqlite, macOS Keychains). ChocoPoC's stealer module collects browser passwords, cookies, autofill and history — scoping the reader to python/sh separates it from the browser itself. Rationale: Uses the exact stealer capability Sekoia listed (browser passwords/cookies/autofill/history) mapped to the concrete on-disk secret stores, gated to a python/shell reader so the browser's own access to those files is excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1555.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser-profile backup/sync scripts written in bash/python
  • Password-manager migration tooling exporting from Chrome/Firefox
  • IT scripted profile cleanup accessing cookie DBs
  • Developer automation using selenium/undetected-chromedriver that copies profile dirs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("backup","rsync","profile-sync-daemon","selenium","chromedriver")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating python/shell is not a sanctioned backup/sync tool — check its command line and parent, and whether it started from a cloned PoC dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, force-reset the user's saved-in-browser and SSO/session credentials (cookies imply session theft), revoke active tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 (Mapbox exfil) for the same host/user, check shell-history and network-config file reads, and expand the browser-store read query across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

Python bulk enumeration of sensitive files (.md/.txt/.db/.sqlite) from PoC context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single Python process reading many distinct .md/.txt/.db/.sqlite files across ≥2 target types in a short window — matching ChocoPoC's stated search for text files, markdown docs and database files. Benign PoC execution does not sweep the filesystem for documentation and DB files. Rationale: Turns the article's explicit collection targets (text, markdown documentation, database files) into a per-process fan-out threshold gated to the python interpreter, which distinguishes a stealer sweep from ordinary PoC file I/O. No Sigma emitted — this is a count/threshold correlation, not single-event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1083 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python static-site/docs generator (mkdocs, sphinx) reading many .md files
  • Data pipeline ingesting many .db/.sqlite/.csv-adjacent files
  • pytest run touching fixture .txt/.db files
  • Backup or indexing script written in Python (e.g. desktop search)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("mkdocs","sphinx","pytest","jupyter","pelican","m>backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review InitiatingProcessCommandLine and working dir — is this a known docs/data tool, or an interpreter under site-packages/a cloned PoC? Inspect SampleFiles for sensitive content (creds, notes, DBs). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and kill the process before exfil completes; preserve the accessed file list. 3) Hunt: correlate the same process/host with UC3 Mapbox egress and UC4 browser-store access to confirm the full ChocoPoC chain, then sweep the fleet for the same fan-out pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where FileName endswith ".md" or FileName endswith ".txt" or FileName endswith ".db" or FileName endswith ".sqlite" or FileName endswith ".sqlite3"
| extend Ext = tostring(extract(@"\.([^.]+)$", 1, FileName))
| summarize DistinctFiles=dcount(FolderPath), DistinctExtTypes=dcount(Ext), SampleFiles=make_set(FileName, 20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctFiles >= 25 and DistinctExtTypes >= 2   // 25 = broad sweep across >=2 of the article's target types
| order by DistinctFiles desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("md","txt","db","sqlite","sqlite3")
| summarize DistinctFiles=dcount(TargetFilePath), DistinctExtTypes=dcount(TargetFileExtension), SampleFiles=make_set(TargetFileName, 20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctFiles >= 25 and DistinctExtTypes >= 2
| order by DistinctFiles desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| ContextImageFileName=/python3?(\.exe)?$/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(md|txt|db|sqlite3?)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(as=FileCount))
| FileCount >= 25

Unpatched Argo CD Repo-Server Flaw Could Let Attackers Take Over Kubernetes Clusters

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Argo CD, a widely used tool for deploying software to Kubernetes, has an unpatched flaw in its repo-server component that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code, provided they can reach the component's internal network port. Synacktiv, which found the bug, says it can lead to a full cluster takeover. There is no fix and no CVE. The firm says it reported the flaw to Argo CD's maintainers in

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Argo CD repo-server exploit: kustomize --helm-command points to non-helm script · [LLM] Argo CD repo-server / kustomize spawning shell or network tooling · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Argo CD service account deploys privileged / host-escape workload · [LLM] New Argo CD Application/ApplicationSet pointing to external Git repo · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ClusterRoleBinding granting elevated rights to Argo CD service account · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Argo CD repo-server exploit: kustomize --helm-command points to non-helm script AIExploitation High
Hunts the Synacktiv unauthenticated RCE against Argo CD repo-server, where an attacker sets kustomize's --helm-command to an attacker-supplied script (pulled from a rogue Git repo) instead of the helm binary. Fires when a kustomize process runs with --helm-command whose target does not resolve to helm. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit primitive — kustomize's --helm-command re-pointed away from the helm binary. Cross-checked with Synacktiv reporting relayed via The Hacker News; legitimate kustomize-with-helm always calls a path ending in 'helm', so a non-helm target is high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/kustomize/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom kustomize helm plugin wrapper script that ends in something other than 'helm' (e.g. a vendored 'helm-wrapper.sh')
  • In-house CI that shims helm via a shell script for private OCI auth
  • Config Management Plugin (CMP) that legitimately templates via a custom binary
  • Debugging/troubleshooting by a platform engineer manually running kustomize with a custom helm path
Suppression filter
| where HelmCmd !in~ ("/custom/bin/helm-wrapper.sh") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the value of --helm-command; confirm whether the target is an approved helm binary path or an unexpected script/temp path. Identify the host — it should be an argocd-repo-server pod/node. 2) Contain: cordon the node, kill the repo-server pod, and apply the Argo CD network policies (networkPolicy.create=true) so only Argo CD components can reach repo-server (TCP 8081) and Redis (6379). Rotate the Redis password. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents from repo-server for egress to attacker Git/registry, check Redis 'mfst' cache integrity, and audit recently synced Applications for attacker-supplied workloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| extend HelmCmd = extract(@"--helm-command[=\s]+([^\s]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(HelmCmd)
| where HelmCmd !endswith "helm" and HelmCmd !endswith "helm.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, HelmCmd, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| extend HelmCmd = extract(@"--helm-command[=\s]+([^\s]+)", 1, TargetProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(HelmCmd) and HelmCmd !endswith "helm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, HelmCmd, TargetProcessCommandLine
title: Argo CD Kustomize helm-command Points to Non-Helm Payload

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*--helm-command*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="--helm-command[=\s]+(?!\S*helm(\s|$))" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*--helm-command*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="--helm-command[=\s]+(?!\S*helm(\s|$))" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Argo CD repo-server / kustomize spawning shell or network tooling AIExploitation High
Detects code execution on the Argo CD repo-server: the parent process argocd-repo-server or kustomize spawning an interactive shell or network utility (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python). This is the observable outcome of the --helm-command RCE where an attacker-controlled script runs in place of helm. Rationale: The repo-server normally only execs git, helm, kustomize and gpg; a shell or curl/wget/nc child is the direct execution artifact of the article's script-injection RCE. Parent-child pairing keeps this far tighter than a bare LOLBin hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/security/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom Config Management Plugins that legitimately shell out to curl/python for private repo auth
  • Init scripts or entrypoint wrappers baked into a custom repo-server image
  • Helm hooks or pre-render scripts that fetch dependency charts via curl/wget
  • Platform-engineer debugging inside the repo-server pod via kubectl exec (would show sh/bash)
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "registry-1.docker.io")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; confirm it is not a known CMP or debugging session (correlate with kubectl exec / DeviceLogonEvents). 2) Contain: kill the repo-server pod, enable Argo CD network policies, and block the repo-server pod's egress to any non-Git/non-Redis destination. 3) Hunt: pivot to the destination IP/URL of any curl/wget, check for a subsequent Redis connection and cache 'mfst' modification, and review new Applications synced after the event.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Argo CD service account deploys privileged / host-escape workload AIInstallation High
Detects the cluster-takeover payload: after poisoning the Argo CD Redis cache, the Argo CD service account syncs a workload whose pod spec requests privileged mode, hostPID/hostNetwork/hostIPC, or a hostPath mount of the Docker/container socket. Targets the Kubernetes API audit trail of the malicious manifest being applied. Rationale: Ties the article's outcome ('Argo CD deployed an attacker-supplied workload') to the concrete host-escape primitives (privileged, hostPID, docker.sock) that a takeover payload needs, scoped to the Argo CD service account as the requestor so normal privileged system pods don't match. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://cycode.com/blog/revealing-argo-cd-critical-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1610 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate privileged DaemonSets (CNI, CSI, node-exporter, Falco) that Argo CD genuinely manages via GitOps
  • A platform team intentionally deploying a privileged monitoring agent through Argo CD
  • hostNetwork ingress controllers deployed by Argo CD
  • Cluster bootstrap/app-of-apps sync that includes system components with hostPath mounts
Suppression filter
| where Namespace !in ("kube-system","monitoring","argocd") and not (Name has_any ("cni","csi","node-exporter","falco","ingress"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the offending manifest against the Git source of truth — if the privileged spec is not in the declared repo, it is Redis cache poisoning. Confirm the source Application and repoURL. 2) Contain: pause auto-sync on the affected Application, delete the malicious workload, rotate the Redis password, and enable network policies isolating repo-server/Redis. 3) Hunt: enumerate all pods created by the argocd SA in the window, check for reverse shells / crypto miners in those pods, and validate no ClusterRoleBinding was added for the argocd SA.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets")
| extend Requestor = tostring(Username)
| where Requestor has "argocd"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ('"privileged":true','"hostPID":true','"hostNetwork":true','"hostIPC":true','/var/run/docker.sock','/var/run/crio/crio.sock','"hostPath"')
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor, Verb, Res, Namespace=tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent, RequestUri

ClusterRoleBinding granting elevated rights to Argo CD service account AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-compromise privilege escalation where a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding is created referencing an Argo CD service account and grants cluster-admin or wildcard verbs, consolidating the 'full cluster takeover' the article warns about. Targets the Kubernetes RBAC audit trail. Rationale: The article's stated impact is 'full cluster takeover', which requires elevated RBAC; a new binding tying the argocd SA to cluster-admin is the highest-fidelity signal of that escalation and rarely happens outside of initial install. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9766-5277-j5hr
ATT&CKT1098 T1548
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial Argo CD install/upgrade via Helm that legitimately binds the argocd application-controller to broad roles
  • GitOps-managed RBAC where the argocd SA role is declared in Git and reconciled
  • Platform team intentionally granting Argo CD cluster-admin for multi-cluster management
  • Disaster-recovery re-provisioning of the Argo CD namespace
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "helm" and Requestor !has "system:serviceaccount:kube-system"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who (user.username / UserAgent) created the binding — an install via 'helm'/'argocd' user agent during a maintenance window is likely benign; an ad-hoc kubectl or the argocd SA itself creating its own escalation is not. 2) Contain: delete the offending ClusterRoleBinding, revoke/rotate the argocd SA token, and enable network policies. 3) Hunt: review all actions taken by the argocd SA after the binding, enumerate new workloads and secrets accessed, and check Redis cache integrity.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings")
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("argocd","argo-cd")
| where ReqStr has_any ("cluster-admin","\"verbs\":[\"*\"]","\"*\"")
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor=tostring(Username), Verb, Res, Name=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent, RequestObject

New Argo CD Application/ApplicationSet pointing to external Git repo AIInstallation Medium
Hunts persistence via a backdoored Argo CD Application: creation or mutation of an applications.argoproj.io / applicationsets.argoproj.io resource whose source repoURL points at an external or untrusted Git host, which would let an attacker continuously reconcile malicious manifests into the cluster. Surfaces the repoURL for analyst triage against the org allowlist. Rationale: The attack reconciles workloads from an attacker-controlled Git repo; monitoring Application/ApplicationSet CRD writes and surfacing repoURL lets analysts spot a source pointed at an untrusted host. Left as hunting because the trusted-repo allowlist is org-specific and cannot be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/security/
ATT&CKT1525 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine GitOps onboarding of a new legitimate Application by the platform team
  • App-of-apps pattern generating many child Applications from a template
  • Developers self-servicing new Applications pointed at approved internal GitLab/GitHub Enterprise
  • Migration of Applications between repos during a repo consolidation
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare RepoURL against the approved Git host allowlist; a public/raw-IP or newly registered domain source is suspicious. Confirm who created it (Requestor/UserAgent). 2) Contain: pause auto-sync and delete the Application if the repo is untrusted; enable network policies. 3) Hunt: inspect the manifests that repo would render (privileged specs, external images), correlate with UC3/UC4, and rotate Argo CD repo credentials given CVE-2025-55190/CVE-2026-42880 secret-exposure history.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("applications","applicationsets")
| extend RepoURL = tostring(RequestObject.spec.source.repoURL)
| extend RepoSources = tostring(RequestObject.spec.sources)
| extend RepoTemplate = tostring(RequestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL)
| where isnotempty(RepoURL) or isnotempty(RepoSources) or isnotempty(RepoTemplate)
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor=tostring(Username), Verb, Res, AppName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), RepoURL, RepoTemplate, RepoSources, UserAgent
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(applications OR applicationsets) (@requestObject.spec.source.repoURL:* OR @requestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL:*)
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("applications","applicationsets") | spath | eval repoURL=coalesce('requestObject.spec.source.repoURL','requestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL') | where isnotnull(repoURL) | table _time user.username verb objectRef.namespace objectRef.name repoURL

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Suspicious MFA Bypass or MFA Reset Activity · [LLM] Credential Stuffing and Brute Force Against Enterprise Accounts · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Lateral Movement via Valid Compromised Credentials · [LLM] Reconnaissance and Information Gathering Pre-Exploitation · [LLM] Bulk data staging and exfiltration via MEGA / rclone · [LLM] Adversary lurking in incident-response chat tools and calls · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious MFA Bypass or MFA Reset Activity AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Scattered Spider's signature MFA-fatigue / push-bombing pattern: a burst of rejected MFA challenges for a single user followed shortly by a successful sign-in, indicating the user (or a help-desk-reset factor) eventually approved an attacker-driven prompt. Article-specific because the crew's core play is talking help desks into resetting/approving logins rather than breaking software. Rationale: Uses the exact Entra/Azure AD MFA-denied result code 500121 followed by a success inside the same fatigue window — the documented Scattered Spider push-bombing + help-desk-reset signature (CISA AA23-320A). Threshold of 5 rejects/hr is above legitimate user behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1621 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely mis-taps 'Deny' several times on a real prompt before approving
  • Authenticator app time-drift causing repeated failed OTP entries then a correct one
  • Shared/service account where multiple humans trigger prompts for the same identity
  • Poor cellular connectivity dropping push notifications until a retry succeeds
  • Newly enrolled device where the user fumbles first-time MFA setup
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in (dynamic(["<corp egress IPs are known-good; add tenant CIDRs>"])) | where Country !in ("<home country>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AccountUpn's sign-in log around FirstDenial–SuccessTime; check the success IPAddress/Country vs the user's baseline and whether a help-desk password/MFA reset preceded it in AuditLogs. 2) Contain: if the success came from a new IP/geo or an unrecognised device, revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), require password reset, and re-verify the MFA method the user actually controls. 3) Hunt: search AuditLogs for 'Update user'/'security info registered' on the same account, and pivot to any post-auth Teams/SharePoint access from the suspicious IP.
let denials = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 500121   // MFA denied / not completed = push-bombing
| summarize DenialCount = count(), FirstDenial = min(Timestamp), LastDenial = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DenialCount >= 5;      // 5 rejected pushes/hr = fatigue attempt (P99 legit <=2)
let successes = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country;
denials
| join kind=inner successes on AccountUpn
| where SuccessTime between (FirstDenial .. LastDenial + 30m)
| project AccountUpn, FirstDenial, LastDenial, DenialCount, SuccessTime, IPAddress, Country
| order by LastDenial desc
let denials = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500121"   // MFA denied / not completed
| summarize DenialCount = count(), FirstDenial = min(TimeGenerated), LastDenial = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DenialCount >= 5;
let successes = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, LocationDetails;
denials
| join kind=inner successes on UserPrincipalName
| where SuccessTime between (FirstDenial .. LastDenial + 30m)
| project UserPrincipalName, FirstDenial, LastDenial, DenialCount, SuccessTime, IPAddress, LocationDetails
| order by LastDenial desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:500121

Credential Stuffing and Brute Force Against Enterprise Accounts AIExploitation Medium
Detects password-spray / credential-stuffing bursts against Entra ID: a single source IP producing invalid-credential failures across many distinct user accounts within an hour. Grounds the article's 'hacking charges' and the group's documented large-scale credential abuse into an actionable identity detection. Rationale: Pivots on Entra failure code 50126 (bad credentials) aggregated by source IP with a distinct-user fan-out threshold — the canonical spray shape. 20 distinct victims/IP/hr is well above any single legitimate misconfigured client. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured on-prem app or MFA server retrying stale creds for many mailboxes from one NAT egress
  • Corporate VPN/NAT gateway aggregating many users behind one IP after a mass password expiry
  • Legacy IMAP/POP client farm with cached bad passwords post rotation
  • Pen-test / red-team password-spray engagement
  • SSO migration causing bulk auth failures from a single connector IP
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in (dynamic(["<corp NAT/VPN egress CIDRs>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the source IP's ASN/geo and whether it matches a known corporate egress; list the targeted users and check if any subsequently succeeded from the same IP. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the identity provider / Conditional Access named-location, and force reset on any account that authenticated successfully from it. 3) Hunt: search for the same IP in successful sign-ins (ResultType 0) and for follow-on MFA-registration or Teams/SharePoint access from those sessions.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 50126   // invalid username or password
| summarize TargetedUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), FailedAttempts = count(), Users = make_set(AccountUpn, 50) by IPAddress, Country, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where TargetedUsers >= 20   // >=20 distinct users sprayed from one IP/hr
| order by TargetedUsers desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50126"   // invalid username or password
| summarize TargetedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FailedAttempts = count(), Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 50) by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where TargetedUsers >= 20
| order by TargetedUsers desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:(50126 OR 50053 OR 50055)

| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.user) as TargetedUsers count as FailedAttempts from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.signature_id="50126" by Authentication.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where TargetedUsers>=20 | sort - TargetedUsers
Lateral Movement via Valid Compromised Credentials AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces post-compromise use of valid credentials by flagging a single account that successfully signs in from multiple distinct IPs or countries within a short window — the impossible-travel / concurrent-session pattern Scattered Spider produces once inside. Complements the credential-access detections by catching the movement that follows a help-desk-driven reset. Rationale: Anti-baseline of successful (ResultType 0) sign-ins fanning out across IPs/countries per account per hour is the cleanest 'stolen valid credential in active use' signal; no invented columns, works on both Entra schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1021.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User on corporate VPN/ZTNA that egresses through multiple regional PoPs
  • Mobile user roaming between cellular and Wi-Fi networks with different public IPs
  • Legitimate frequent traveller or a user plus their MDM-managed devices in different networks
  • Cloud/SaaS service accessing on the user's behalf from datacentre IPs
  • Household with dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 flipping public addresses
Suppression filter
| where IPs !has_any ("<corporate VPN egress CIDRs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: map each IP to ASN/geo and device; confirm whether the geos are physically reconcilable and whether any IP is a hosting/VPN provider common to Scattered Spider. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and require re-auth with a phishing-resistant method; if a hosting-provider IP is present, block it via Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: from the suspect IP/session, pivot to DeviceLogonEvents for RDP/SSH (LogonType RemoteInteractive) into sensitive hosts and to any privileged-role assignment in AuditLogs.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize IPCount = dcount(IPAddress), CountryCount = dcount(Country), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where CountryCount >= 2 or IPCount >= 5   // same account, many geos/IPs within an hour
| order by IPCount desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)

| where CountryCount >= 2 or IPCount >= 5
| order by IPCount desc

| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.src) as IPCount values(Authentication.src) as IPs from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where IPCount>=5 | sort - IPCount
Reconnaissance and Information Gathering Pre-Exploitation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a burst of internal directory/domain enumeration (net group, nltest, adfind, Get-AD* cmdlets) from a single interactive user account — the recon Scattered Spider runs after gaining a foothold to locate admins and sensitive shares. Hunts the specific reconnaissance tooling, not generic PowerShell use. Rationale: Ties named recon binaries (nltest, adfind) and specific Get-AD* cmdlets to a per-user hourly burst threshold, excluding machine accounts — high-signal for hands-on-keyboard enumeration rather than routine admin scripting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1087.002 T1482
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin or helpdesk running net group / Get-ADGroupMember for legitimate access reviews
  • Monitoring/IAM tooling enumerating AD on a schedule under a service account
  • SCCM/Intune or vulnerability scanner performing domain discovery
  • Onboarding scripts querying groups for new-hire provisioning
  • Security team's own AD-audit tooling (e.g. PingCastle, BloodHound collector by IT)
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("<sanctioned admin/service accounts>") | where DeviceName !in~ ("<known admin jump hosts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the AccountName is a sanctioned admin/service identity and whether the host is an admin jump box; review the full command set for trust/DC enumeration. 2) Contain: if the account is a standard user, disable it and isolate the device pending review. 3) Hunt: pivot from the same account/host to subsequent lateral logons, credential-access tooling, and archive/exfil binaries (rclone, 7z) to place this recon in a kill chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("group \"domain admins\"","group /domain","user /domain","group \"enterprise admins\""))
    or (FileName =~ "nltest.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/domain_trusts","/dclist","/trusted_domains"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADGroup","Get-ADGroupMember","Get-ADComputer","Get-ADDomainController"))
    or (FileName =~ "adfind.exe")
| summarize CmdCount = count(), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where CmdCount >= 5   // burst of directory recon in one hour
| order by CmdCount desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Proc = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where (Proc endswith "\\net.exe" or Proc endswith "\\net1.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("group \"domain admins\"","group /domain","user /domain")
    or Proc endswith "\\nltest.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("/domain_trusts","/dclist")
    or (Proc endswith "\\powershell.exe" or Proc endswith "\\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADGroup","Get-ADComputer","Get-ADDomainController")
    or Proc endswith "\\adfind.exe"
| summarize CmdCount = count(), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine, 20) by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where CmdCount >= 5
| order by CmdCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\nltest.exe OR *\\adfind.exe OR *\\NET.EXE OR *\\NLTEST.EXE OR *\\ADFIND.EXE) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*Get-ADUser* OR *Get-ADGroup* OR *Get-ADComputer*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\(net|net1|nltest|adfind)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(\/domain|domain admins|domain_trusts|\/dclist)/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/Get-AD(User|Group|GroupMember|Computer|DomainController)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count())
| _count >= 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as Cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","adfind.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("*Get-ADUser*","*Get-ADGroup*","*Get-ADComputer*","*Get-ADDomainController*"))) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=5 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as Cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","adfind.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("*Get-ADUser*","*Get-ADGroup*","*Get-ADComputer*","*Get-ADDomainController*"))) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=5 | sort - count
Bulk data staging and exfiltration via MEGA / rclone AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Scattered Spider's documented exfiltration tooling — rclone and MEGA clients, plus password-protected archive creation with 7-Zip/WinRAR — used to stage and move copied corporate data before extortion. Directly supports the article's account of intruders copying a retailer's data and demanding ~$8M. Rationale: rclone and MEGA (megacmd/MEGAsync) are explicitly named Scattered Spider exfil tools in CISA AA23-320A; pairing them with password-protected archive flags (-hp/-p/-mx) keys the article's 'copied its data' claim to concrete, rare-in-user-space binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT team legitimately using rclone for sanctioned cloud backup/migration
  • Developers or users making password-protected 7-Zip/WinRAR archives for routine transfers
  • Backup software invoking Compress-Archive in scheduled jobs
  • A user with a personal MEGAsync install syncing non-corporate files
  • DevOps pipelines archiving build artifacts with -mx compression
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("<sanctioned backup/migration operators>") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("<approved backup agent>.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the command line for the remote target (rclone 'mega:'/'remote:' config, archive output path) and correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections to mega.nz / user.mega.co.nz. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block MEGA/rclone destinations at the proxy/firewall; preserve the staged archive for scoping. 3) Hunt: identify which shares/DBs were read before the archive, check for the same tool on other hosts, and review the initiating account for a preceding help-desk reset or anomalous sign-in.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe")
    or (FileName in~ ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (" a "," -hp"," -p ","-mx"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Compress-Archive")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Proc = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where Proc has_any ("\\rclone.exe","\\megacmd.exe","\\megasync.exe","\\mega.exe")
    or (Proc has_any ("\\7z.exe","\\7za.exe","\\winrar.exe","\\rar.exe") and CommandLine has_any (" a "," -hp"," -p ","-mx"))
    or (Proc has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Compress-Archive")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scattered Spider Data Exfiltration Tooling (rclone/MEGA/archive)
id: 7f3c1e2a-8b4d-4c6e-9a1f-2d5b6c7e8f90
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of rclone, MEGA clients or password-protected archive creation used by Scattered Spider for bulk data staging and exfiltration.
references:
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/19-year-old-scattered-spider-suspect.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1567.002
  - attack.t1560.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tools:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\rclone.exe'
      - '\megacmd.exe'
      - '\megasync.exe'
      - '\mega.exe'
  selection_archive:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\7z.exe'
      - '\7za.exe'
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - ' -hp'
      - ' -p '
      - '-mx'
  condition: selection_tools or selection_archive
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\rclone.exe OR *\\Rclone.exe OR *\\megacmd.exe OR *\\MEGAcmd.exe OR *\\megasync.exe OR *\\MEGAsync.exe OR *\\mega.exe) OR (@Image:(*\\7z.exe OR *\\7za.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\rar.exe) AND @CommandLine:(* a * OR *\-hp* OR *\-mx*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\(rclone|megacmd|megasync|mega)\.exe$/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(7z|7za|winrar|rar)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s(a|-hp|-p|-mx)/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/Compress-Archive/i)
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as Cmds min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("* a *","*-hp*","*-p *","*-mx*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Compress-Archive*")) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as Cmds min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("* a *","*-hp*","*-p *","*-mx*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Compress-Archive*")) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - firstTime
Adversary lurking in incident-response chat tools and calls AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the article's distinctive Scattered Spider tradecraft: once inside, intruders lurk in the victim's collaboration tools and join breach-response meetings to watch defenders. Flags an account reading/listing messages across an unusually large number of distinct Teams channels/chats in a short window — collection of IR chatter rather than normal use. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's specific claim that intruders 'lurk in a company's chat tools and join the calls it holds to respond to the breach'; a per-account hourly fan-out across many Teams objects is an abnormal collection pattern distinct from routine messaging. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1213.005 T1580
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Compliance/eDiscovery or DLP tooling enumerating Teams content under a service account
  • A community manager or exec assistant who legitimately monitors many channels
  • Teams admin performing a migration or bulk export
  • Automated bot/connector indexing messages for search
  • New employee catching up across many onboarding channels on day one
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("<eDiscovery/compliance service accounts>","<Teams admin accounts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the account is a sanctioned compliance/admin/bot identity; review which channels were accessed — flag any named 'incident', 'IR', 'breach', or exec crisis channels. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, revoke Teams sessions, disable the account, and move breach-response coordination to an out-of-band channel the adversary cannot see. 3) Hunt: correlate the account with a preceding help-desk MFA reset or anomalous sign-in, and check for guest/external members recently added to IR channels.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in ("MessagesListed","MessageRead","ChatRetrieved","MeetingParticipantDetail")
| summarize DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectId), Ops = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctObjects >= 15   // reading across >=15 channels/chats in an hour = harvesting
| order by DistinctObjects desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in ("MessagesListed","MessageRead","ChatRetrieved","MeetingParticipantDetail","MemberAdded")
| summarize DistinctChannels = dcount(ObjectId), Ops = count(), OpSet = make_set(Operation, 10) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctChannels >= 15
| order by DistinctChannels desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent

| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
